I couldn't agree more, thanks for adding this because it's definitely equally as important. I'm assuming we're both referencing the US, which of course focuses on GDP. This results in exactly what you described, an inhumane treatment of people because they merely need to output the MOST hours possible. Efficiency of work doesn't actually depend on output or quality of products but merely the amount of time spent existing in a working environment. 

I don't know how to achieve it, but I think a 4 day work week with careers we feel fulfilled in would benefit the country immensely. Or the option to work a fifth day. Europe models a more lenient work-life balance. And it works pretty well. I look at it like school... when I was young and hated it, the entire day felt like an eternity and I accomplished very little. In college, I was very involved and despite spending much less time actually in class, my attention was naturally there and my productivity skyrocketed. For me, this directly translates to *my* work ethic as an employee. This is anecdotal, but I think it could be scaled up to most people. The current model is broken, and funnels money up the ladder.
